title: Simple Interest Basics
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Principal, rate, time, amount and the SI formula

introduction.overview: Interest is the price paid for using someone else's money. When you deposit money in a bank, the bank pays you interest; when you take a loan, you pay interest. In simple interest the interest is calculated only on the original sum (the principal) for every period, so it grows by the same amount each year. Four quantities are linked: principal P, rate R per cent per year, time T in years, and simple interest SI.
introduction.placementRelevance: Simple interest is commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, usually as a one-step formula question or a two-condition problem such as "the sum doubles in 8 years". It is also the stepping stone to compound interest in Year 2.
introduction.realWorldContext: A bank fixed deposit that pays a flat rate on the original deposit, an education loan with monthly flat interest, and a post-office saving scheme are everyday uses of simple interest.

learningObjectives: Use SI = P × R × T / 100 to find any one of the four quantities
Find the amount A = P + SI and work backwards from the amount
Convert months and days into years correctly
Solve "sum doubles or triples" and "same sum at two rates" problems
Split a sum between two rates and handle borrowing-and-lending gains

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: R% per year means R rupees for every 100 rupees per year. Converting time: 6 months = 6/12 = 0.5 year, 73 days ≈ 73/365 = 0.2 year.

coreDefinitions: Principal (P): the original sum of money lent or borrowed.
Rate (R): the interest paid on every ₹100 for one year, written R% per annum (p.a.).
Time (T): the period for which the money is lent, expressed in years.
Simple interest (SI): the interest calculated on the principal alone, SI = P × R × T / 100.
Amount (A): the total money to be paid back or received, A = P + SI.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: In simple interest the same amount of interest is earned every year. If ₹1,000 earns ₹80 in the first year, it earns ₹80 in the second year and again in the third. The interest therefore grows in a straight line with time, like a taxi meter running at a fixed rate.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: To find SI, ask "how much on ₹100 in one year?" That is R. Then scale by P/100 for the principal and by T for the years. For ₹5,000 at 8% for 3 years: 5000/100 = 50 hundreds, each earning 8 × 3 = 24, so SI = 50 × 24 = ₹1,200.

importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The master formula linking all four quantities.

importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Total amount at the end of the period.
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: When the question gives or asks for the final amount.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Rearranged forms
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Solve for whichever quantity is missing.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Doubling and tripling
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: If a sum becomes n times itself in T years, R = 100(n − 1)/T

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Time in months and days
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The rate is always per year.

mainNarrative: Identify the three known quantities from P, R, T and SI (or A), and plug them into the one formula. The most common source of error is not the formula but the unit of time. Convert to years before substituting.

When the amount is given instead of the interest, subtract the principal. If an amount of ₹7,500 after 2 years and ₹8,250 after 3 years is given, the difference ₹750 is the interest of exactly one year, so the principal is 7500 − 2 × 750 = ₹6,000 and the rate is 750/6000 = 12.5%.

For "a sum becomes n times itself" use SI = (n − 1) × P. Doubling means the interest equals the principal. If doubling takes 8 years, the interest for one year is P/8, so R = 12.5% p.a. Tripling in the same rate takes twice as long, 16 years, because tripling needs interest of 2P.
In borrowing-and-lending problems, the gain or loss is the difference of the two interest amounts, which is P × (difference of rates) × T / 100.

deepDiveAspects.title: SI is linear in every variable
deepDiveAspects.content: Doubling the principal, the rate or the time doubles the interest. This lets you scale a known answer instead of recomputing from scratch. If ₹1,000 gives ₹120 interest, then ₹3,000 for the same period at the same rate gives ₹360.

deepDiveAspects.title: Why simple interest is only a first model
deepDiveAspects.content: Real accounts usually add interest to the principal each period, called compound interest. Simple interest is the special case where the interest is not reinvested, and it is the right model for flat-rate loans.

solvedExamples.title: Direct simple interest
solvedExamples.question: Find the simple interest on ₹5,000 at 8% per annum for 3 years, and the amount.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: SI = P × R × T / 100 and A = P + SI.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Every year earns 8% of ₹5,000 = ₹400, and three years earn ₹1,200.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Giving the amount when the question asks only for the interest, or the reverse.

solvedExamples.title: Principal and rate from two amounts
solvedExamples.question: A sum of money amounts to ₹7,500 in 2 years and ₹8,250 in 3 years at simple interest. Find the sum and the rate.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: The increase between consecutive years equals one year's simple interest.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Simple interest is the same every year, so the difference of the two amounts is one year's interest.

solvedExamples.title: Splitting a sum between two rates
solvedExamples.question: ₹7,000 is lent partly at 6% and the rest at 4% per annum. The total yearly interest is ₹360. Find the part lent at 6%.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Interest from the 6% part + interest from the 4% part = ₹360.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Check: 6% of 4000 = 240 and 4% of 3000 = 120, which total ₹360.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Using the same rate for both parts.

shortcutMethods.title: Hundreds method

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Multiply P × R × T into a large number and then divide by 100.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Divide P by 100 first to count the hundreds, then multiply by R × T. ₹5,000 at 8% for 3 years: 50 hundreds × 24 = ₹1,200.

rulesForApplication: Cancel the 100 against P before multiplying.
A sum that becomes n times in T years has R = 100(n − 1)/T.
For months, write T as a fraction, e.g. 8 months = 2/3 year.
The gap between amounts of two consecutive years is one year's interest.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Stopping at the interest when the amount was asked.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Re-read the last line of the question before writing the final answer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the amount as the principal
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Substituting A in place of P.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Subtract the interest first or use the difference of amounts.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Treating R as a decimal when it is a percentage.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Always keep the /100 in the formula.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Estimate the interest as principal × rate (%) × years / 100. Options far from this estimate can be dropped immediately.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: SI is one of the quickest topics. Direct SI and doubling questions should be solved in under a minute.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Companies mix SI with ratio, for instance by lending two parts at different rates, so practise the equation set-up as well.

summaryBullets: SI = PRT/100 and A = P + SI.
Convert time to years before substituting.
Doubling in T years means R = 100/T.
Difference of consecutive-year amounts = one year's SI.
Gain on borrow-and-lend = P × (rate difference) × T / 100.

keyTakeaways: There are only four quantities; know any three to find the fourth.
Simple interest is the same every year.
Read whether SI or amount is wanted.
selfCheckQuestions: Can I find the rate if a sum triples in 20 years?
